fixes.explanation: Right. Moses tells Aaron and his sons Eleazar and Ithamar not to let their hair become disheveled or tear their garments. But the people get to grieve, because “…the whole house of Israel, may mourn…” over the fire. So the priests hold steady at their post while all of Israel is free to mourn.

Not quite, friend. Moses is speaking to Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar, and he tells them not to let their hair become disheveled or tear their garments. Then he says that “the whole house of Israel” may mourn over the fire the LORD ignited. So mourning isn't shut down for everybody. The instruction not to mourn that way is for Aaron and his sons.

A head count sounds like a fine job for a priest, friend, but this verse doesn't give it as the reason. The LORD links knowing holy from common and clean from unclean to teaching the Israelites His statutes. You can't teach a recipe you don't know yourself. I'd be a terrible teacher if I couldn't tell dough from crumbs.

Angry is right. Moses went looking carefully for the goat of the sin offering and found it burned up. The text says he was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron's remaining sons. His next question shows what bothered him: why wasn't it eaten in the holy place, when it was given to take away the guilt of the congregation (Lev 10:17)?

That's the question. Moses had asked why the sin offering wasn't eaten in the holy place, and Aaron answers with a question of his own. He points out that his sons presented their sin offering and burnt offering that very day, and that these things had happened to him. I think he means the loss of Nadab and Abihu. Then he asks whether eating the sin offering that day would have been acceptable in the LORD's sight.

Satisfied is right. Remember Moses was angry back in verse 16 when he found the goat burned up. Then Aaron explained himself, and that was enough. The anger is gone by the end of the passage. I wish every kitchen argument ended with one honest answer like that.
